title: Extension of relative rational group homomorphisms
statement: Let $S$ be any scheme [def-pc-scheme], and let $G,H$ be smooth separated finite-type $S$-group schemes [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Group scheme means multiplication, identity and inverse morphisms over $S$ satisfying the group-object diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] with $S$ as base; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Products and fibres are scheme-theoretic base changes [def-pc-base-change]. An $S$-dense open is one dense in every fibre. Let $U\subset G$ be $S$-dense and open [def-weil-open-immersion], and let $a:U\to H$ be an $S$-morphism. Assume that the two morphisms $a(xy)$ and $a(x)a(y)$ agree on an $S$-dense open in the domain $\{(x,y)\in U\times_SU:xy\in U\}$ of $a(xy)$. Then there is a unique $S$-group homomorphism $\bar a:G\to H$ restricting to $a$ on $U$. In particular, if an $S$-birational map between $G$ and $H$ is compatible with multiplication as a rational map, it extends to a unique $S$-group isomorphism. Here $S$-birational means represented by an isomorphism between $S$-dense opens, and rational equality means equality on an $S$-dense common open. No normality, Noetherianity or field hypothesis on $S$ is imposed.

proof.text: We use the following density calculation throughout. A smooth map is flat and locally finitely presented, hence universally open. Thus, for a smooth $S$-map $p:Y\to Z$ and an $S$-dense open $A\subset Z$, every nonempty open $W\subset Y_s$ has nonempty open image $p_s(W)$, which meets $A_s$; hence $p^{-1}(A)$ is $S$-dense in $Y$. Finite intersections of dense opens are dense, also inside any open. Base changes and open restrictions of smooth maps are smooth, and their composites are smooth, by the cited statements. For a smooth $S$-scheme $Y$, every $S$-dense open is schematically dense by the smooth-density node, including after arbitrary base change. Consequently two $S$-morphisms $Y\to H$ agreeing on such an open are equal by the relative scheme-theoretically dominant separated-target lemma. That lemma needs only separatedness of $H\to S$, not reducedness of $S$ or $Y$.

proof.text: Put $C_0=U\times_SU$, $q:C_0\to G$, $q(x,y)=xy$, and $b:C_0\to H$, $b(x,y)=a(x)a(y)$. The automorphism $\tau:G\times_SG\to G\times_SG$, $(x,y)\mapsto(xy,y)$, has inverse $(z,y)\mapsto(zy^{-1},y)$; these identities are group-object identities and hold as morphisms. Thus multiplication is the first projection after $\tau$, and is smooth by smooth base change and invariance under isomorphisms. Restricting its source to $C_0$ gives a smooth $q$. Also $C_0$ is smooth over $S$, by base change, open restriction and composition. For any geometric point $g$ of $G$, over a geometric base point $s$, the opens $U_s$ and $(U_s)^{-1}g$ are dense in $G_s$: base change preserves density, and inverse and translation are isomorphisms. Their intersection is nonempty, since $G_s$ contains $g$. Choosing a geometric point $y$ there gives $x=gy^{-1}\in U_s$ and $xy=g$. Thus every geometric fibre of $q$ is nonempty, so $q$ is surjective. This does not require connected fibres or rational points over the residue field.

proof.text: Let $C_U=q^{-1}(U)\subset C_0$. This is smooth over $S$ by open restriction. The hypothesis gives an $S$-dense open of $C_U$ on which $b=a\circ q$. By schematic density and separated-target equality, these two morphisms agree on all of $C_U$. Moreover $C_U$ is $S$-dense in $C_0$, by the open-image calculation of step 1 applied to $q$ on each fibre.

source.place: 5.1 Proposition 3 proof: rational compatibility; 2.5 Lemma 1(b), schematic density

proof.text: Form the actual scheme-theoretic kernel pair $R=C_0\times_G C_0$, with projections $r_1,r_2$, and put $h=q r_1=q r_2$. Each $r_i$ is smooth, being a base change of $q$; hence $R\to S$ and $h:R\to G$ are smooth by composition. The open $R_U=h^{-1}(U)$ is $S$-dense in $R$ by step 1. On $R_U$, step 3 gives $b r_1=a h=b r_2$ as morphisms. Since $R$ is smooth over $S$, $R_U$ is schematically dense; separated-target equality therefore gives $b r_1=b r_2$ on all of $R$. This proves precisely the compatibility required for morphism descent, including nilpotents on the overlap.

source.place: 5.1 Proposition 3 proof, with the overlap check for its use of 2.5 Proposition 5 made explicit

proof.text: The singleton $\{q\}$ is an fpqc covering in the stated covering convention, even when $U$ is not quasi-compact. Indeed $q$ is flat and universally open by smoothness. For every affine open $A\subset G$, take affine opens in $q^{-1}(A)$ covering it. Their images are open in $A$ and cover $A$ by surjectivity. Quasi-compactness of the affine scheme $A$ gives finitely many such affine opens whose images cover $A$, exactly the definition of an fpqc covering. Apply representable fpqc descent to $b$ and step 4 to obtain a unique morphism $\bar a:G\to H$ with $\bar a q=b$. Its composite with $H\to S$ equals $G\to S$, since both composites agree after the fpqc cover $q$ and uniqueness of representable descent applies with target $S$. Thus $\bar a$ is an $S$-morphism.

On $C_U$, step 3 and the descent equation give $\bar a q=a q$. The base change $q_U:C_U\to U$ is smooth and surjective (its geometric fibres are the fibres of $q$ over points of $U$), so the fpqc-cover argument in step 5 applies to $q_U$. Uniqueness in representable descent implies $\bar a|_U=a$ on the entire prescribed open $U$, rather than merely on a smaller rational domain.

source.place: 2.5 Proposition 5, restriction of the descended morphism; Stacks 023Q (lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms)

proof.text: Let $W=(U\times_SU)\cap m_G^{-1}(U)$ in $G\times_SG$. Each of the two projections and $m_G$ is smooth, so step 1 makes $W$ $S$-dense in the smooth $S$-scheme $G\times_SG$. On $W=C_U$, steps 3 and 6 show $\bar a(xy)=\bar a(x)\bar a(y)$. Schematic density and relative separated-target equality extend this identity to all of $G\times_SG$. On every test $S$-scheme the resulting multiplicative map between groups sends the identity to an idempotent, hence to the identity, and then sends inverses to inverses by cancellation. These are natural identities, so they give the unit and inverse diagrams as morphisms. Finally any other $S$-morphism extending $a$ equals $\bar a$ by schematic density of $U$ in $G$ and the same relative equality lemma. This proves the required homomorphism and its uniqueness.

source.place: 5.1 Proposition 3, printed pp.113-114: extension preserves the group law and is unique; 2.5 Lemma 1(b)

proof.text: For the final clause choose an isomorphism $\alpha:U_0\simeq V_0$ between $S$-dense opens representing the birational map, and let $A:G\to H$ be its homomorphism extension just proved. The open $W_0=(U_0\times_SU_0)\cap m_G^{-1}(U_0)$ is $S$-dense in $U_0\times_SU_0$ by step 1. Its image $E_0$ under $\alpha\times\alpha$ is therefore $S$-dense in $V_0\times_SV_0$. For $(v,w)=(\alpha(x),\alpha(y))$ in $E_0$, multiplicativity gives $vw=\alpha(xy)\in V_0$, and hence $\alpha^{-1}(vw)=xy=\alpha^{-1}(v)\alpha^{-1}(w)$. These are identities of morphisms on $E_0$, not just equalities of geometric points. Since $E_0$ is dense in $V_0\times_SV_0$, it is dense in the open domain of the left side. The proved extension result therefore applies to $\alpha^{-1}$, giving $B:H\to G$. The composites $BA$ and $AB$ agree with the identities on $U_0$ and $V_0$ respectively, hence agree everywhere by schematic density and relative separated-target equality, using separatedness of both $G$ and $H$. Thus $A$ is the unique group isomorphism extending the birational map.
